
An automated cascade either finds a grant recipient in the IRS Business Master
File or it does not. [Adjudicating the MAYBE
tier](adjudicating-maybe.html) is about the cases where it found several
candidates and could not choose. This one is about the cases where it found
nothing worth offering — and the first thing to say is that most of them are
not matching failures at all.

**Of 91 randomly drawn NO identities, 53 are payees the Business Master File
could never contain.** Individuals collecting scholarships, businesses,
government bodies, foreign organisations, and placeholders like `SEE SCHEDULE
ATTACHED`. Only 33 are organisations the file should list and the cascade
missed. The honest floor — real bodies with no exemption of their own — is 6.

## The tier this is about

```{r}
tab(status_tbl, col.names = c("status", "identities", "share of 4,903", "meaning"))
```

### 845, not 725

The published baseline reports **725** NO. `pf_status()` reports **845**, and
the gap is the interesting part.

```{r}
tab(no_shape)
```

`pf_status()` runs over every identity in the file. The tiered result runs only
over identities that got at least one scored candidate. 120 in-scope
identities never reached the result frame because no blocking pass produced any
pair at all — and so the baseline's denominator of 4,748 **excludes the cases
retrieval failed on hardest**.

```{r}
tab(den_tbl)
```

On the in-scope denominator the same run is 61.20%, not 62.74%. That is not a
defect in the arm; it is a statement about which figure answers which
question. A match rate cannot drop the grants its retrieval step never reached.
Everything below is reported against 4,868.

## Why there is no *no-search* arm

The MAYBE experiment compared a cheap model, an expensive one, and the
expensive one with web search, because all three could answer its question: the
correct EIN was already in the candidate set 71% of the time, so a reviewer
confined to the packet had something real to decide.

Here it is not. A NO case has no candidate worth offering, so **when there is
an answer it is outside the packet 100% of the time.** A model without search
can only report that the filed name does not resemble the records already
rejected, which is what the cascade said. So every arm on this tier has search.

An earlier version of this page went further and said no cheaper strategy was
benchmarked because none applied. That was two claims in one sentence and only
the first holds. A cheaper *model* with search applies perfectly well; it had
simply not been run.

### It was run, and it reproduces the findings

Haiku 5.5 on the same 100 cases, through the same case renderer and the
same collection code — the arm is parameterised by model, not forked, so the
two arms cannot drift apart in anything but the model.

```{r}
tab(arms_tbl)
```

The overlap is near-total: **30 found by both arms, 3 by Opus only, none by
Haiku only.** All three Opus-only cases are `SALVATION ARMY`, where Haiku
identified the organisation and then declined to name an EIN — for an ambiguous
local corps against a national body that is the defensible answer rather than a
failure to search. And where both arms named an EIN, **they named the same one
31 times out of 31.**

The taxonomy this page publishes survives the substitution:

```{r}
tab(arms_tax_tbl)
```

`entity_class` agrees exactly on the two classes that carry the headline —
`INDIVIDUAL` 39 and 39, `NONPROFIT` 27 and 27. `miss_hypothesis` is the
weakest, which is what the most speculative field in the schema should do: it
asks the model to guess *why* a match failed, the one question it cannot check
against a source. Both arms also flag the same single reference absence,
Commonwealth University of Pennsylvania. Two independent runs agreeing on which
one record the BMF is right to omit is worth more than either run alone.

So the breakdowns below do not rest on the expensive model.

### The saving is 5x, not 40x

Haiku 5.5 lists at \$0.10/\$0.50 per MTok against Opus 5.5's \$4/\$20, which
invites an expectation of a 40-fold saving. The measured ratio is **5.1x**, for
two reasons that only show up once the run is instrumented for them.

Haiku prices a request by its *whole prompt*, stepping to \$0.50/\$2.50 above
100K tokens, and **22 of the 100 cases crossed that step** — which is what a
web-search turn does. Banking the run's totals against the cheap rate would
have reported about \$0.46 and understated by nearly three times. Second, the
cheap arm ran **37% more searches**, and searches are billed per use and are in
neither figure.

And once those per-use searches are counted, the 5.1x does not survive
multiplication either. Projected over the whole tier
(`dev/adjudicate-18-layer-costs.R`):

```{r}
tab(bill_tbl)
```

Search is **77% of the cheap arm's bill and 32% of the expensive one's**,
because the cheap arm ran more of them. On the full invoice the expensive model
costs **1.73x**, not 5.1x, and over the tier the model choice is worth about
\$33,000 against a search budget worth about \$35,000.

So the cost lever on this tier is `max_uses`, not the model. The cheap model is
still the one to use — 33.0% against 36.3% recovered, and the *same EIN* 31
times out of 31 where both named one — but it should be chosen on the evidence
that it is nearly as good, not on a price ratio that shrinks by a factor of
three when the bill is added up. `dev/DEVELOPMENT-PLAN.md` §"Phase 4b" works
through the layer choice for both tiers.

## What a reviewer is given

The filed record — name, street, city, state, ZIP, stated purpose, amount, tax
year, and the foundation's own recipient-status text, all uncontrolled filer
free text. The filing foundation, as context. And then one of two things:

- **no candidate retrieved** (12 of the 100 cases): nothing to show, the
  reviewer works from the filed record alone
- **the rejected near-misses, with their scores** (88 cases): the records the
  cascade found and declined

The near-misses are shown deliberately. In the prior hand audit the correct
record had *already been offered* in most recoverable cases, so hiding them
would hide the dominant mechanism.

They are also a trap, and the schema is built around it. An EIN read off a
near-miss row is in the reference **by construction** — it got there because
the blocker pulled it out of the reference — so counting it as evidence that
the reference covers this tier is circular. Every verdict therefore records
whether its EIN came from the web or from a candidate row, and the headline
uses web-sourced EINs only.

As it happened, **all 34 EINs in the estimation stratum were web-sourced and
none was read off a candidate row**, so the guard had nothing to exclude. That
was not guaranteed; it is why it was built.

## How much of the tier is recoverable

```{r}
tab(recover_tbl, col.names = c("", "n", "share", "95% Wilson"))
```

That projects to **~306 of the 845** NO identities, [229, 393].

"Recoverable" here means: the investigation established an EIN from an outside
source, and that EIN is in the reference. It is a mechanical set-membership
test — the model never saw the reference and was told so. It is **not** a
verified match: an EIN can be in the reference and still belong to the wrong
organisation. The head-to-head below is the only check on that.

### Is the right EIN already in the reference?

This is the question that decides whether the NO tier is a coverage problem or
a name problem.

| | in the reference |
|---|---|
| estimation stratum | 33 of 34 — 97.1% |
| both strata | **37 of 38 — 97.4%** [86.5%, 99.5%] |

The single exception is `COMMONWEALTH UNIV OF PENN`, EIN 23-2738930, which the
model classed `GOVERNMENT` — a Pennsylvania state university. A governmental
unit is not an exempt organisation, so the file is **correct** to omit it.

**Zero genuine coverage gaps in 38 independently established EINs.** The
earlier audit found 21 of 21 on a narrower population; this confirms it on the
production tier at nearly double the n. Widening the reference will not shrink
this residual, because the reference already contains it.

## Why the cascade missed them

For the 37 recoverable cases, was the correct EIN ever put in front of the
scorer? Every scored pair is cached, so this is a lookup rather than a replay
of the blocker.

```{r}
tab(why_tbl)
```

Where it *was* offered, the score the comparator gave the correct row was a
median of **0.360**, ranging 0.080 to 0.622, against a review floor of 0.65.
Only 2 of 26 reached even 0.60.

So the dominant failure is not retrieval. In 70% of recoverable cases the right
record was in hand and ranked far below the floor.

```{r}
tab(miss_tbl)
```

Two patterns are worth naming.

**A misspelling is never retrieved at all.** `THE WESMINSTER SCHOOL` and
`COCORDIA UNIVERSITY` scored *no* candidates — `n_cand = 0`, `n_pairs = 0`. So
did `THE PASSONISTS`, which the model filed under `DBA_OR_TRADE_NAME` but which
fails the same way (`PASSONISTS` against `PASSIONIST`), making the real count
**3 of 91 rather than 2**.

What carries this is the mechanism, not the sample: three cases could not
support the word "never" on their own. Every pass in the cascade is exact
equality — `name_key` or `dba_key` plus ZIP5 or state, a shared name token
within state, an exact name anywhere, initials, an 18-character prefix plus
ZIP5 — and npmatch has no approximate comparator at the blocking stage at all.
A one-character edit in the one distinctive token therefore leaves no key
anywhere, while `SCHOOL` and `UNIVERSITY` are pruned out as too frequent. No
comparator can rescue a case that never reaches it. This is the subject of the
next section.

**`PARENT_OR_CHAPTER` is always retrieved and always underscored.** Four of the
five are `SALVATION ARMY` and `YOUNG LIFE` at 0.08 — a name that cannot
discriminate between hundreds of real records, where the geography term
correctly refuses to break the tie. These should *not* be forced through:
loosening there buys wrong EINs.

The two call for opposite fixes, which is why reporting them as one "name
resolution" number would be useless.

## The one failure no reviewer can fix, and the cheapest fix in the package

Pursuing those three cases turned out to answer a larger question than the one
it was asked.

**The correct record is in the reference at the filed ZIP5.** Not merely
present — present in the block the cheapest pass in the whole cascade already
looks at:

```{r}
tab(typo_tbl)
```

Pass A1 blocks on name plus ZIP5 and misses each of them by one letter.

### Why no adjudication pass can help, at any price

This is worth stating plainly because it is the natural next question.
Adjudication *ranks a candidate sheet*. For these cases the sheet is empty, so
Opus, Haiku or a human reading it sees nothing to choose between. A cheaper
adjudicator, a more expensive one and a better-instructed one all return the
same thing. The failure is upstream of the stage.

Both search arms did recover them, because search goes outside the packet. But
paying a model to search the web for a missing letter is an expensive answer to
a question string distance answers for nothing.

### Jaro-Winkler inside a ZIP5 block

`pf_fuzzy_candidates()` scores the filed `name_key` against the reference rows
sharing its ZIP5, falling back to city plus state where that block is empty,
and emits the best few above a cutoff. Blocking first is what makes it free:
the pools are small — median 505 reference rows on this sample, largest 2,930 —
and one pool takes microseconds against the 223,151 candidates pass B2
generates on 5,000 grants.

It does not reimplement any decision. `npmatch::np_block()` returns nothing but
a frame of row indices, which `np_compare()` accepts directly, so the pairs go
through the same comparator, selector and tiering as every exact pass and a
fuzzy pair clears the same bar.

All three misspellings rank **first** in their own ZIP5 pool, at 0.941, 0.924
and 0.857. At the 0.90 default **two of the three clear** —
`THE WESMINSTER SCHOOL` to 58-0566206 at score 0.930, `COCORDIA UNIVERSITY` to
39-0833608 at 0.923.

The third is the honest limit of the pass, and it is worth following because it
fails twice for two different reasons. `THE PASSONISTS` sits at 0.857, below
the cutoff. Lower the cutoff to 0.85 and it *is* offered, with the correct EIN
— 22-2092362, the one search established — and then the scorer rejects it at
**0.360**. `PASSONISTS` against `PASSIONIST MISSIONARIES INC` is a weak name
match once the comparator reads the whole string rather than the prefix.

So lowering the cutoff moves that case from "never retrieved" to "retrieved and
rejected". That is a better failure — it is visible to a reviewer and countable
in the diagnostics — but it is not a recovery, and no cutoff makes it one.

### The cutoff is set from the collision, not from the recall

Scoring all 91 cases against their ZIP5 pools gives both halves of the
trade-off at once:

```{r}
tab(cutoff_tbl)
```

The default is **0.90**, and the reason is the right-hand column rather than
the left. The highest similarity any individual's name reaches is **0.854** —
`ALEXANDER SCHWEIG` against `ALEXANDER GRAHAM BELL`. A cutoff of 0.85 sits
*underneath* that collision, which is why the margin column goes negative: at
0.85 the threshold is no longer separating organisations from individuals.

That near-collision is structural, not bad luck. Jaro-Winkler's prefix bonus is
precisely what rewards a shared first name, so individuals — 39 of these 91
cases, 43% of the tier — are the population this comparator is worst at
excluding.

And the five recoveries between 0.90 and 0.85 are offers, not clearances. On
the full-file regression the pass clears **24** identities to YES at 0.90 and
**25** at 0.85 — one more identity for 1,105 more pairs and a cutoff below the
personal-name collision. There is essentially no recall left to buy.

**What protects the individuals is the cutoff, not the `skip_personal` flag.**
That is worth stating carefully, because the obvious reading is the other way
round. Scanning all 39 with the flag disabled:

```{r}
tab(personal_tbl, col.names = c("", "n", "reach 0.85", "reach 0.90",
                             "highest", "median"))
```

At the 0.90 default **no individual reaches the cutoff at all**, flagged or
not. The flag fires on only 11 of the 39 — 28% recall, though with no false
positives on this sample — so 28 individuals go into the pool regardless, and
they top out at 0.809. `skip_personal` is defence in depth rather than the
primary control. It earns its place by catching the one case that does cross
0.85, but n=1 is not a basis for leaning on it, and a cutoff that needed it to
work would be the wrong cutoff.

**There are no false offers at any cutoff**, which is the column most likely to
be misread. The nearest thing to one is `SEE SCHEDULE ATTACHED` against `SEE
SCHEDULE O` at 0.91 — two placeholders are near-identical strings describing
nothing — and the placeholder filter removes it on both sides before the
comparator runs. The zero in that column is the filter working, not an absence
of near-collisions, which is one more reason the pass does its own filtering
rather than trusting a threshold.

### What it is not limited to

It runs on the **residual**, which is every identity that has not cleared YES —
845 NO *and* 1,044 MAYBE. "NO" is a tier assigned after scoring, so it cannot
be blocked on, and `np_cascade()` drops an identity from its pending set only
when a pass clears it to YES, which is the same rule. So the pass changes the
MAYBE tier too: it adds rows to the adjudication queue and can change which row
a MAYBE identity holds.

The YES set is protected by construction rather than by a threshold — an
identity that has cleared is not in the residual, no pair is added to it, and
its selection cannot move. `pf_fuzzy_recover()` asserts that instead of
trusting it, and `dev/adjudicate-16-fuzzy-regress.R` re-checks it
independently.

### What it does to a full run

These 91 cases cannot say what the pass does to everything else, because it was
designed on them. The regression runs the production configuration end to end
over all 4,868 in-scope identities:

```{r}
tab(regress_tbl)
```

**+0.49 points** of clear rate at the default, for about 9% of the match time
it supplements — and no identity that had cleared YES moved at any cutoff,
which is the assertion rather than a hope. 0.85 buys **one** identity over 0.90
for 1,105 more pairs and a cutoff below the personal-name collision. The scan
computes every similarity in the block and then filters, so the cutoff barely
changes what it costs.

The fourth column is the one worth pausing on. Three of the 24 identities the
pass clears at the default **had no candidate at all** beforehand — no blocking
pass produced a single pair for them, so there was nothing on a review sheet to
look at and nothing for any adjudicator to rank. Those are the cases this pass
exists for, and they are invisible in a clear-rate delta.

> That run uses the matchdb `active-observed` tier (6.67M rows), not the
> augmented reference the rest of this article is measured on (3.88M). Every
> cached bundle predates an npmatch reinstall and `pf_check_reference()`
> correctly refuses them, so the reference was rebuilt from the current default
> tier rather than silently matching against stale keys. Its tier counts are
> therefore **not** comparable to the 62.74% quoted elsewhere here; what they
> measure is what the pass does to a full run on the reference the pipeline now
> uses by default.

### The one case that argues against it

Of the 33 EINs search established, the pass reaches 3 at the default and lands
the same EIN on 2. The third is the finding, not a footnote: one identity
cleared to **YES on 36-3641111** where search established **36-4703871**, at
score 0.874 and similarity 0.914 — comfortably inside the range the pass treats
as good. One of the two is wrong and the pipeline has no way to tell which.

That is the cost of the seam that makes the pass cheap. Because a fuzzy pair
goes through the same scorer and tiering as an exact pair, it can be
*confidently* wrong in the same way, and the pass has no notion of having
guessed. One contradiction out of three is not a rate, but it is the right
shape of warning, and it wants checking by hand before the pass is leaned on at
scale.

### What it does not replace

It reaches 3 of the 33 — the typo class, and nothing else. The other 30 are
legal-name changes, DBAs, parent/chapter structure and acronyms, where the
filed string and the reference string are not near-neighbours under any
character metric and no cutoff helps. Those still need a reviewer or a model
with search. What the pass removes is the subset that never needed either.

## What lives outside the BMF, and why

```{r}
tab(class_tbl)
```

Rolled up by whether a record should exist at all:

```{r}
tab(group_tbl, col.names = c("", "n", "share", "95% Wilson"))
```

### Not an organisation (58.2%)

The largest group in the tier by a wide margin. 39 individuals — almost all
scholarship payments to named students — plus 5 government bodies (a high
school, a public elementary school, a county fire and rescue department, a
state university, a university research institute), 5 foreign organisations (a
Polish foundation, UNIDROIT, a UK charity, a BC society, the ICRC), 3 aggregate
placeholders, and 1 for-profit.

These reached the matching path, where they can only fail or match something
wrong. **They are a denominator problem, not a matching problem.**

And the pipeline's own signals largely did not catch them:

```{r}
tab(flag_tbl)
```

Every case `looks_personal` flagged really is an individual — 11 of 11, no
false positives — and it misses 28 of 39. A precise, low-recall flag is the
easy kind to fix: nothing needs to become more conservative, the 202-name
given-name list simply has to get longer. Seven payees that are not
organisations at all are affirmatively coded `public_charity` by the filed
status field, which is why that field cannot be trusted on its own.

### A real body with no exemption of its own (6.6%)

The honest floor. Two churches (`SEVIER HEIGHTS BAPTIST CHURCH`, `ST AGNES
CHURCH`), which are exempt without applying and need not file; a diocesan high
school under a group ruling; one fiscally sponsored project; and two named
events. There is no EIN to find, so no amount of matching recovers these.

At 6.6% this is **much smaller** than the prior audit's 12-in-100 estimate for
the same category. The floor is a few percent, not a tenth.

### Could not be identified at all (0%)

Search identified something in every one of the 91 cases. The prior audit,
which searched 46 of its 67 adjudicated cases, had 10 "no such organisation
traceable". With search applied to every case that category disappears.

### Why `entity_class` and `bmf_expectation` are separate fields

The `INTERNATIONAL COMMITTE OF THE RED CROSS` case earns the distinction. The
model classed it `FOREIGN`, which is right — it is Swiss — and
`bmf_expectation` `LISTED`, which is also right, because it holds a US
exemption record. The EIN it reported is in the reference.

Collapsing "what the entity is" into "should a record exist" would have scored
that case wrong whichever way it collapsed. A Scout troop is a subordinate and
is not listed; a Salvation Army area command is a subordinate and is. They are
different questions.

## Does a human agree?

Almost everything above is the model's judgement, so it needs a check against
something other than the model's own confidence.

An earlier hand audit adjudicated 67 NO cases. Re-keyed on the filed recipient
name, 63 of them are still NO identities in this arm, so the same arm was run
over exactly those 63 and the two sides compared. Both judged the same
organisations from the same filed record; the only difference is who judged.

```{r}
agree_tbl <- data.frame(
  class = c("not an organisation", "a real body the BMF should list",
            "no exemption of its own", "could not be identified"),
  recall = c("11 of 11", "30 of 34", "5 of 6", "3 of 8"),
  pct = c("100.0%", "88.2%", "83.3%", "37.5%"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
tab(agree_tbl, col.names = c("human's class", "model agreed", ""))
```

Overall **49 of 59 — 83.1%** [71.5%, 90.5%], Cohen's kappa **0.724**. Four
cases the human marked unclear are excluded; a non-answer cannot agree or
disagree with anything.

Three of the ten disagreements exist only because this comparison maps the
human's "geography unclear" verdict to *recoverable*. All three are churches.
Dropping that hedge gives 87.5% and kappa 0.795 — the figure above keeps the
conservative reading.

### The one class they diverge on is the reassuring part

37.5% on "could not be identified" looks alarming until the cases are read. Of
the 8 the human could not trace, the model agreed on exactly 3 — and those 3
are precisely the ones where it reported **low confidence and named no
organisation**.

On the other 5 it found something at medium or high confidence. `DOCKS TO
DOORWAYS` is a Belgrade Lakes Association campaign, and the filed street field
literally reads `PO Box 551 Belgrade Lakes Associati[on]`. `AMERICAN SHRINE
ASSOCIATES` sits at the Basilica of the National Shrine's address. `505 Main
Street Canton` is not a name at all, it is a street address, and the depot
there is run by a food pantry.

**The model's confidence tracks the disagreement exactly**: where it says low it
agrees the case is untraceable, and where it says medium or high it found what
the human could not. That is the opposite of the pattern the [MAYBE search
arm](adjudicating-maybe.html) showed, where confidence rose while accuracy
fell. Here confidence is worth routing on.

### On the EIN itself, which needs no vocabulary mapping

Both sides name an EIN on 24 cases and give **the same nine digits on 23 —
95.8%**. The exception is `The Salvation Army`: the model gives the Illinois
corporation, the human the Southern territory. Both EINs are real; which is
correct depends on which corporation received the money.

The model named an EIN on 11 cases where the human could not, and **all 11 are
in the reference** — 5 of them cases the human had already called a real
organisation without being able to produce its number.

The human named one where the model declined: `Hamilton Co Gen Hlt Dist`. It is
a county health district, the model called it government, and that EIN is the
one human EIN *not* in the reference. The model was right to refuse it.

### Both sides land in the same place

| | recoverable, of the same 63 |
|---|---:|
| human | 34 — 54.0% |
| model | 35 — 55.6% |

| | independently established EINs in the reference |
|---|---|
| model | **33 of 33 — 100%** |
| human | 24 of 25 — 96.0% |

Neither side found a single genuine coverage gap.



## Where that leaves the match rate

```{r}
tab(rate_tbl)
```

Recovering the NO tier is worth **+6.29 points**. But dropping the payees that
are not organisations the file could ever hold — ~492 identities, taking the
denominator from 4,868 to 4,376 — moves YES alone from 61.20% to **68.08%**, a
gain of **+6.88 points**, while matching precisely nothing.

The scope correction is worth more than the recovery. Only one of the two is a
matching improvement; the other is a statement about which grants were ever
answerable. Both should be reported, and neither should be quietly folded into
a headline.

## What this does not establish

- **Recoverability is not accuracy.** 36.3% of the tier has an EIN that exists
  in the reference. Whether it is the *correct* EIN rests on the head-to-head
  above and on the model's own confidence, not on the set-membership test.
- **The taxonomy is a model's judgement.** The mechanical parts — is the EIN in
  the reference, was it ever offered, what did it score — are not. The split
  between them is deliberate and the two should not be quoted with equal
  confidence.
- **One adjudicator on each side.** The human labels come from a single pass
  with no blind second review, and the model ran once at one effort level.
  Neither is a consensus.
- **`UNCERTAIN` was barely used.** One case of 100. A reviewer that almost
  never declines is either very well calibrated or is resolving ambiguity it
  should be surfacing; 100 cases cannot separate those.
- **The 120 never-scored identities are 12 cases in this sample.** Their
  composition is reported with everything else, but a 12-case subset supports
  no claim of its own.
- **Search cost is not in the token figure.** $0.0669 per case in tokens for
  Opus and $0.0131 for Haiku, plus 3.2 and 4.4 web searches per case billed
  separately. No ratio to the MAYBE arms is quoted: those were computed on that
  experiment's own runs, some logged before the cache-write accounting was
  corrected.
- **Two models agreeing is not two models being right.** The arms match on 31
  of 31 EINs and on the single reference absence, which is evidence against
  independent error, not against *shared* error. Both were given the same
  instructions and both read the same web.
- **The misspelling class is three cases.** The fix below is validated on 3 of
  91, and what carries it is the mechanism — every blocking pass is exact
  equality — not the sample size. Its 0.90 cutoff is set from 91 cases and 38
  personal names, which is enough to see the collision and not enough to price
  it precisely.

## Reproducing

```
PFMATCH_DIR=. Rscript dev/adjudicate-10-no-packet.R    # re-runs the match, ~30 min
Rscript dev/adjudicate-11-no-search.R
Rscript dev/adjudicate-12-no-score.R

PF_NO_SET=cal Rscript dev/adjudicate-10-no-packet.R    # the human head-to-head
PF_NO_SET=cal Rscript dev/adjudicate-11-no-search.R
Rscript dev/adjudicate-14-no-calib.R

PF_NO_MODEL=claude-haiku-5-5 PF_NO_TAG=-haiku Rscript dev/adjudicate-11-no-search.R
PF_NO_TAG=-haiku Rscript dev/adjudicate-12-no-score.R  # the cheap arm
Rscript dev/adjudicate-15-no-arms.R                    # Haiku vs Opus

Rscript dev/adjudicate-16-fuzzy-regress.R              # the fuzzy pass, full file
Rscript dev/adjudicate-17-fuzzy-cutoff.R               # the cutoff table
Rscript dev/adjudicate-18-layer-costs.R                # what each layer costs
```

The packet stage gates every identity's tier against `BASELINE-2026-10C` and
stops on any drift, because a sample drawn from a drifted run does not describe
the baseline's NO tier and its recovery could not be added to the baseline's
match rate. It also re-checks that it drew the same 100 ids as the cached
packet, so a rebuild cannot silently leave collected verdicts keyed to
different case text.

Design, full read-out and the taxonomy definitions are in
`dev/NO-TIER-EXPERIMENT.md`; the reviewer's instructions are
`dev/LLM-NO-INSTRUCTIONS.md`.
